questions.question: Which planet is the largest in our solar system?
questions.explanation: Jupiter is the largest planet in our solar system by both mass and diameter.

questions.question: What is the capital city of Canada?
questions.explanation: Ottawa is the capital of Canada and is located in the province of Ontario.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel 'Pride and Prejudice'?
questions.explanation: Jane Austen wrote Pride and Prejudice, which was first published in 1813.

questions.question: Which element has the chemical symbol Au?
questions.explanation: Au is the chemical symbol for gold, derived from the Latin word aurum.

questions.question: In which year did the first modern Olympic Games take place?
questions.explanation: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens, Greece, in 1896.

questions.question: Which ancient civilisation built Machu Picchu?
questions.explanation: Machu Picchu was built by the Inca civilisation in the 15th century in what is now Peru.

questions.question: Which country has the largest land area in the world?
questions.explanation: Russia is the world's largest country by total land area.

questions.question: Which sport uses the terms 'love', 'deuce' and 'advantage'?
questions.explanation: Love, deuce and advantage are commonly used scoring terms in tennis.

questions.question: What is the chemical formula for water?
questions.explanation: Each water molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom.

questions.question: Which planet is known as the Red Planet?
questions.explanation: Mars looks red because its surface is covered in iron oxide, better known as rust.

questions.question: How many legs does a spider have?
questions.explanation: All spiders have eight legs, which is one way to tell them apart from six-legged insects.

questions.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air to make their food?
questions.explanation: Plants use carbon dioxide, water and sunlight to make sugar, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

questions.question: What is the hardest natural substance on Earth?
questions.explanation: Diamond scores 10, the top of the Mohs hardness scale, and is made entirely of carbon.

questions.question: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?
questions.explanation: An adult heart beats around 100,000 times a day.

questions.question: At what temperature does water boil at sea level?
questions.explanation: Water boils at 100°C, or 212°F, at sea level; it boils at lower temperatures up mountains.

questions.question: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star; the next closest, Proxima Centauri, is over 4 light years away.

questions.question: What do bees collect from flowers to make honey?
questions.explanation: Bees turn sugary nectar into honey by adding enzymes and fanning it with their wings to dry it out.

questions.question: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.explanation: Roots are covered in tiny root hairs that greatly increase the area for soaking up water.

questions.question: Which force keeps our feet on the ground?
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls every object with mass towards every other; Earth's pull keeps us grounded.

questions.question: How many bones are in the adult human body?
questions.explanation: Babies are born with around 300 bones, many of which fuse together as they grow.

questions.question: Which gas makes up most of Earth's atmosphere?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the air; oxygen is about 21%.

questions.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
questions.explanation: An adult's skin weighs around 4 kg and covers about 2 square metres.

questions.question: Which scientist developed the theory of general relativity?
questions.explanation: Einstein published general relativity in 1915, describing gravity as the bending of space and time.

questions.question: What is the chemical symbol for sodium?
questions.explanation: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name for sodium.

questions.question: Which planet has the largest and brightest ring system?
questions.explanation: All four giant planets have rings, but Saturn's, made of ice and rock, are by far the most spectacular.

questions.question: Which part of a cell is often called its 'powerhouse'?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria turn food into energy the cell can use, and carry their own DNA.

questions.question: Which blood type is known as the universal donor?
questions.explanation: O negative red cells can be given to almost anyone, so hospitals use them in emergencies.

questions.question: Roughly how fast does light travel?
questions.explanation: At about 300,000 km per second, light from the Sun takes around 8 minutes to reach Earth.

questions.question: Who created the first vaccine, against smallpox?
questions.explanation: In 1796 Jenner used cowpox to protect against smallpox; 'vaccine' comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.question: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
questions.explanation: Mercury melts at −39°C; gallium melts at about 30°C, just warm enough to melt in your hand.

questions.question: Who discovered penicillin in 1928?
questions.explanation: Fleming noticed that mould growing on a dish had killed the bacteria around it.

questions.question: Which large galaxy is expected to collide with the Milky Way?
questions.explanation: Andromeda and the Milky Way are expected to merge in about 4.5 billion years.

questions.question: Which part of the brain mainly controls balance and coordination?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum sits at the back of the brain and holds more than half of its neurons.

questions.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
questions.explanation: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and the third pumps it around the rest of the body.

questions.question: Roughly what is the half-life of carbon-14?
questions.explanation: Carbon-14's half-life of about 5,730 years is what makes radiocarbon dating work.

questions.question: Which planet rotates on its side, tilted at about 98 degrees?
questions.explanation: Uranus was probably knocked over by a huge collision early in the solar system's history.

questions.question: What is the capital of France?
questions.explanation: Paris has been France's capital for most of the last thousand years.

questions.question: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Pacific covers about a third of Earth's surface, more than all the land combined.

questions.question: On which continent is Kenya?
questions.explanation: Kenya lies on the equator in East Africa, on the coast of the Indian Ocean.

questions.question: In which country is the Taj Mahal?
questions.explanation: The Taj Mahal in Agra was built by Emperor Shah Jahan as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal.

questions.question: What is the capital of Japan?
questions.explanation: Kyoto was Japan's capital for over a thousand years before Tokyo took over in 1869.

questions.question: Which river flows through London?
questions.explanation: The Thames runs about 346 km from the Cotswolds to the North Sea.

questions.question: Which European country is shaped like a boot?
questions.explanation: The island of Sicily sits just off the 'toe' of Italy's boot.

questions.question: What is the highest mountain in the world above sea level?
questions.explanation: Everest stands about 8,849 m tall on the border of Nepal and China.

questions.question: What is the largest hot desert in the world?
questions.explanation: The Sahara covers about 9 million square km, roughly the size of the United States.

questions.question: In which country is the city of Rio de Janeiro?
questions.explanation: Rio was Brazil's capital until Brasília took over in 1960.

questions.question: In which city does the Statue of Liberty stand?
questions.explanation: The statue stands on Liberty Island in New York Harbor and was dedicated in 1886.

questions.question: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as the capital, partly as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne.

questions.question: What is the longest river in South America?
questions.explanation: The Amazon carries more water than any other river, about a fifth of all river water reaching the sea.

questions.question: What is the smallest country in the world by area?
questions.explanation: Vatican City covers just 0.44 square km, entirely within the city of Rome.

questions.question: What is the capital of Turkey?
questions.explanation: Ankara became the capital in 1923, although Istanbul is Turkey's largest city.

questions.question: Which mountain range is traditionally part of the border between Europe and Asia?
questions.explanation: The Urals run about 2,500 km north to south through western Russia.

questions.question: Which African country was once known as Abyssinia?
questions.explanation: The name Abyssinia was widely used in Europe until the mid-20th century.

questions.question: What is the capital of New Zealand?
questions.explanation: Wellington is the world's southernmost capital of a sovereign state.

questions.question: Which strait separates Spain from Morocco?
questions.explanation: At its narrowest the Strait of Gibraltar is only about 14 km wide.

questions.question: What is the longest river in Europe?
questions.explanation: The Volga flows about 3,500 km through Russia into the Caspian Sea.

questions.question: In which country is Mount Kilimanjaro?
questions.explanation: At 5,895 m, Kilimanjaro is Africa's highest mountain and the world's tallest free-standing one.

questions.question: What is the capital of Brazil?
questions.explanation: Brasília was built from scratch in the 1950s and laid out in the shape of an aeroplane.

questions.question: Counting overseas territories, which country spans the most time zones?
questions.explanation: Thanks to territories from the Pacific to the Indian Ocean, France covers 12 time zones.
questions.reviewNote: Counts depend on what's included: France is usually given 12, Russia and the US 11.

questions.question: What is the name of the deepest known point in Earth's oceans?
questions.explanation: Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, is nearly 11 km below the surface.

questions.question: In which country is Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake?
questions.explanation: Baikal holds around a fifth of the world's unfrozen fresh surface water.

questions.question: Which river flows through Baghdad?
questions.explanation: The Tigris and Euphrates enclose Mesopotamia, one of the birthplaces of civilisation.

questions.question: The Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, is mostly in which country?
questions.explanation: Some weather stations in the Atacama have never recorded rain.

questions.question: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
questions.explanation: Lesotho is the only country in the world that lies entirely above 1,000 m.

questions.question: In which year did the Titanic sink?
questions.explanation: The Titanic sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg in April 1912.

questions.question: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Armstrong stepped onto the Moon on 20 July 1969, with Buzz Aldrin following shortly after.

questions.question: In which year did the Berlin Wall fall?
questions.explanation: The wall had divided East and West Berlin since 1961; Germany reunified the following year.

questions.question: Who was the first President of the United States?
questions.explanation: Washington took office in 1789 and served two terms.

questions.question: In which city is the ancient Colosseum?
questions.explanation: The Colosseum opened in AD 80 and could hold around 50,000 spectators.

questions.question: In which year did the Second World War end?
questions.explanation: The war ended in Europe in May 1945 and in Asia that September.

questions.question: Which queen of ancient Egypt had a famous romance with Mark Antony?
questions.explanation: Cleopatra was the last active ruler of Egypt's Ptolemaic dynasty.

questions.question: Who was the British Prime Minister for most of the Second World War?
questions.explanation: Churchill took over from Chamberlain in May 1940.

questions.question: The Great Wall was built to protect which country?
questions.explanation: Walls were built and rebuilt over around 2,000 years; most of what stands today dates from the Ming dynasty.

questions.question: Who gave the famous 'I Have a Dream' speech in 1963?
questions.explanation: King spoke to about 250,000 people at the March on Washington.

questions.question: Which explorer reached the Americas in 1492?
questions.explanation: Columbus was trying to reach Asia by sailing west, and landed in the Bahamas.

questions.question: Which French leader was defeated at the Battle of Waterloo?
questions.explanation: After his defeat in 1815, Napoleon was exiled to the remote island of Saint Helena.

questions.question: Which ship carried the Pilgrims to America in 1620?
questions.explanation: The Mayflower took about two months to cross the Atlantic, with 102 passengers aboard.

questions.question: In which year did the First World War begin?
questions.explanation: The war began in the summer of 1914, weeks after Archduke Franz Ferdinand was assassinated.

questions.question: Who was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize?
questions.explanation: Curie won the Physics prize in 1903 and the Chemistry prize in 1911.

questions.question: Which civilisation built the city of Tenochtitlan?
questions.explanation: Tenochtitlan was built on an island in a lake; Mexico City stands on its site today.

questions.question: Which English king had six wives?
questions.explanation: Henry's wives are often remembered by the rhyme 'divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived'.

questions.question: In which country did the Industrial Revolution begin?
questions.explanation: It began in Britain in the mid-1700s, driven by coal, steam power and textile mills.

questions.question: Who was the first person to travel into space?
questions.explanation: Gagarin orbited Earth once in 1961, in a flight lasting 108 minutes.

questions.question: In which year was the Battle of Hastings fought?
questions.explanation: William of Normandy's victory at Hastings led to the Norman conquest of England.

questions.question: Which charter, sealed in 1215, limited the power of the English king?
questions.explanation: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede, beside the River Thames.

questions.question: Which South African leader was released from prison in 1990?
questions.explanation: Mandela spent 27 years in prison and became South Africa's president in 1994.

questions.question: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still stands?
questions.explanation: The Great Pyramid is the oldest of the seven wonders and the only one left.

questions.question: Who was the first emperor of Rome?
questions.explanation: Julius Caesar never became emperor; his adopted heir Augustus took the role in 27 BC.

questions.question: In which year did the French Revolution begin?
questions.explanation: The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 is still celebrated as France's national day.

questions.question: How long did the Hundred Years' War actually last?
questions.explanation: The war between England and France ran on and off from 1337 to 1453.

questions.question: Which civilisation invented cuneiform writing?
questions.explanation: The Sumerians pressed wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets over 5,000 years ago.

questions.question: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic?
questions.explanation: Earhart flew from Newfoundland to Northern Ireland in 1932.

questions.question: How many players does a football team have on the pitch?
questions.explanation: Each side fields ten outfield players and a goalkeeper.

questions.question: In which sport would you perform a slam dunk?
questions.explanation: A slam dunk is when a player jumps and forces the ball down through the hoop.

questions.question: How many rings are on the Olympic flag?
questions.explanation: The five interlocking rings stand for the five inhabited continents taking part in the Games.

questions.question: How many minutes long is a standard football match?
questions.explanation: A match is two 45-minute halves, plus any time added on for stoppages.

questions.question: Which sport is played with a shuttlecock?
questions.explanation: Top players can smash a shuttlecock at over 400 km/h, faster than anything else hit in a racket sport.

questions.question: How many holes are played in a standard round of golf?
questions.explanation: The 18-hole round was set at St Andrews in Scotland in 1764.

questions.question: In which sport might you score a try?
questions.explanation: A try is scored by touching the ball down over the opponent's goal line.

questions.question: In boxing, what does 'KO' stand for?
questions.explanation: A knockout means a boxer can't get up before the referee counts to ten.

questions.question: Which city hosted the 2012 Summer Olympics?
questions.explanation: London became the first city to host the modern Summer Olympics three times.

questions.question: In golf, what is a score of one under par on a hole called?
questions.explanation: Two under par is an eagle, and three under is an albatross.

questions.question: How many points is a touchdown worth in American football?
questions.explanation: After a touchdown, the team can try for one or two extra points.

questions.question: In which sport do teams compete for the Stanley Cup?
questions.explanation: The Stanley Cup, first awarded in 1893, is the oldest trophy in North American professional sport.

questions.question: In snooker, which ball is worth the most points?
questions.explanation: The black is worth seven points, which is why a maximum break is 147.

questions.question: What does the overall leader of the Tour de France wear?
questions.explanation: The yellow jersey matches the yellow paper of L'Auto, the newspaper that started the race.

questions.question: In cricket, how many balls are in a standard over?
questions.explanation: Eight-ball overs were once used in Australia and elsewhere, but six is now standard.

questions.question: What is the highest score possible with three darts?
questions.explanation: Three treble 20s make 180; 170 is the highest score you can finish a leg on.

questions.question: How long is a marathon?
questions.explanation: The odd distance was fixed after the 1908 London Olympics, whose route started at Windsor Castle.

questions.question: In which sport is the Ryder Cup played?
questions.explanation: The Ryder Cup is played every two years between teams from Europe and the United States.

questions.question: How many players does a volleyball team have on court?
questions.explanation: Players rotate positions each time their team wins back the serve.

questions.question: Which country did the sport of judo come from?
questions.explanation: Judo was created by Kanō Jigorō in 1882 and means 'the gentle way'.

questions.question: How long is an Olympic swimming pool?
questions.explanation: An Olympic pool holds about 2.5 million litres of water.

questions.question: In baseball, how many strikes make an out?
questions.explanation: Four balls, on the other hand, give the batter a free walk to first base.

questions.question: On which surface is the French Open tennis tournament played?
questions.explanation: It's the only Grand Slam played on clay, at Roland Garros in Paris.

questions.question: How many players does a netball team have on court?
questions.explanation: Each player wears a bib with their position and may only enter certain areas of the court.

questions.question: In which event would an athlete perform the 'Fosbury Flop'?
questions.explanation: Dick Fosbury won Olympic gold with his backwards technique in 1968, and almost everyone now uses it.

questions.question: Which country hosted the first FIFA World Cup in 1930?
questions.explanation: Uruguay also won the tournament, beating Argentina 4–2 in the final.

questions.question: Which martial art's name means 'empty hand'?
questions.explanation: Karate developed in Okinawa, in what is now southern Japan.

questions.question: In which sport is a period of play called a 'chukka'?
questions.explanation: A chukka lasts about seven minutes, and players usually change horses between them.

questions.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
questions.explanation: Leonardo worked on the Mona Lisa for years; it now hangs in the Louvre in Paris.

questions.question: John, Paul, George and Ringo were members of which band?
questions.explanation: The Beatles formed in Liverpool in 1960.

questions.question: Who wrote 'Romeo and Juliet'?
questions.explanation: Shakespeare wrote the tragedy in the mid-1590s; it's set in Verona, Italy.

questions.question: In 'The Wizard of Oz', what colour is the brick road Dorothy follows?
questions.explanation: The yellow brick road leads Dorothy to the Emerald City.

questions.question: Which instrument usually has 88 keys?
questions.explanation: A standard piano has 52 white keys and 36 black keys.

questions.question: Which fictional detective lived at 221B Baker Street?
questions.explanation: Arthur Conan Doyle first introduced Sherlock Holmes in 1887.

questions.question: How many strings does a standard guitar have?
questions.explanation: A standard bass guitar, by contrast, has four strings.

questions.question: Which 1975 Steven Spielberg film is about a great white shark?
questions.explanation: Jaws is often called the first summer blockbuster.

questions.question: Who wrote the Harry Potter books?
questions.explanation: The first book, 'Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone', was published in 1997.

questions.question: What is the name of the cowboy doll in 'Toy Story'?
questions.explanation: Released in 1995, 'Toy Story' was the first feature film made entirely with computer animation.

questions.question: Which country does flamenco come from?
questions.explanation: Flamenco grew up in Andalusia, in southern Spain.

questions.question: Who wrote 'Charlie and the Chocolate Factory'?
questions.explanation: Dahl is said to have been inspired by chocolate companies sending test bars to his school.

questions.question: Who composed the 'Moonlight Sonata'?
questions.explanation: Beethoven didn't name it; a critic compared it to moonlight on a lake after his death.

questions.question: Which painter famously cut off part of his own ear?
questions.explanation: Van Gogh did it in 1888 in Arles, in southern France, and later painted a self-portrait with a bandaged ear.

questions.question: Who painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel?
questions.explanation: Michelangelo painted the ceiling between 1508 and 1512, mostly standing on scaffolding.

questions.question: Which novel begins with the line 'Call me Ishmael'?

answers.A: The Old Man and the Sea

questions.explanation: Herman Melville's Moby-Dick, published in 1851, follows the hunt for a white whale.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel '1984'?
questions.explanation: The book gave us terms like 'Big Brother' and 'thoughtcrime'.

questions.question: What was Disney's first full-length animated film?

answers.A: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs

questions.explanation: Snow White was released in 1937, and many in Hollywood expected it to flop.

questions.question: Which instrument did jazz legend Louis Armstrong famously play?
questions.explanation: Armstrong was also known for his gravelly singing voice, as in 'What a Wonderful World'.

questions.question: In which Shakespeare play is the line 'To be, or not to be'?
questions.explanation: Prince Hamlet speaks the line while thinking about life and death.

questions.question: Who painted 'Girl with a Pearl Earring'?
questions.explanation: Vermeer painted it around 1665; it hangs in the Mauritshuis in The Hague.

questions.question: Which singer was known as 'the King of Rock and Roll'?
questions.explanation: Elvis had his first big hit, 'Heartbreak Hotel', in 1956.

questions.question: In Mary Shelley's novel, who creates the monster?
questions.explanation: The monster has no name in the book; 'Frankenstein' is its creator.

questions.question: Who composed 'The Four Seasons'?
questions.explanation: Vivaldi's four violin concertos were published in 1725, one for each season.

questions.question: Who wrote the novel 'War and Peace'?
questions.explanation: The novel follows Russian families through Napoleon's invasion of 1812.

questions.question: Which art movement is Salvador Dalí most associated with?
questions.explanation: Dalí's melting clocks in 'The Persistence of Memory' are among Surrealism's best-known images.

questions.question: In which language was Mozart's opera 'The Magic Flute' written?
questions.explanation: Most operas of the time were in Italian, but Mozart wrote 'Die Zauberflöte' in German.

questions.question: Which ancient poet is said to have written 'The Iliad' and 'The Odyssey'?
questions.explanation: The poems tell of the Trojan War and Odysseus's ten-year journey home.

questions.question: How many days are in a leap year?
questions.explanation: The extra day, 29 February, keeps the calendar in line with Earth's orbit of about 365.25 days.

questions.question: What colour do you get by mixing blue and yellow paint?
questions.explanation: Blue and yellow are two of the traditional primary colours used by painters.

questions.question: How many sides does a hexagon have?
questions.explanation: Bees build hexagonal honeycomb because the shape fits together with no gaps and little wax.

questions.question: What is the largest animal that has ever lived?
questions.explanation: Blue whales can grow over 30 m long, bigger than any known dinosaur.

questions.question: What is the fastest land animal?
questions.explanation: A cheetah can reach around 100 km/h, but only in short bursts.

questions.question: How many colours are traditionally listed in a rainbow?
questions.explanation: Isaac Newton named seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.

questions.question: What is a baby kangaroo called?
questions.explanation: A newborn joey is about the size of a jellybean and crawls into its mother's pouch.

questions.question: How many weeks are in a year?
questions.explanation: 52 weeks makes 364 days, so a year is always a day or two longer.

questions.question: What is the main ingredient of guacamole?
questions.explanation: Guacamole comes from Mexico; its name comes from the Aztec word for avocado sauce.

questions.question: In which country did pizza originate?
questions.explanation: The modern pizza comes from Naples, where the Margherita was named after Queen Margherita in 1889.

questions.question: What is a group of lions called?
questions.explanation: A pride is usually a few related females, their cubs and one or two males.

questions.question: Which animal is called the 'ship of the desert'?
questions.explanation: Camels can go for days without water, and their wide feet don't sink into the sand.

questions.question: How many years are in a millennium?
questions.explanation: Millennium comes from the Latin mille, meaning thousand, and annus, meaning year.

questions.question: At what temperature does water freeze in Fahrenheit?
questions.explanation: Water freezes at 32°F and boils at 212°F, exactly 180 degrees apart.

questions.question: What is the Roman numeral for 50?
questions.explanation: C is 100, D is 500 and V is 5.

questions.question: What is the currency of Japan?
questions.explanation: The word yen means 'circle' or 'round object' in Japanese.

questions.question: In the NATO phonetic alphabet, which word stands for the letter D?
questions.explanation: The alphabet, from Alpha to Zulu, helps letters be heard clearly over radio.

questions.question: What is the square root of 144?
questions.explanation: 144 is also known as a gross, meaning a dozen dozens.

questions.question: What is the longest bone in the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur, or thigh bone, is about a quarter of a person's height.

questions.question: What is a word that reads the same backwards called, like 'level'?
questions.explanation: Palindrome comes from Greek words meaning 'running back again'.

questions.question: What does 'www' stand for in a web address?
questions.explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN.

questions.question: How many squares are there on a chessboard?
questions.explanation: A chessboard is an 8 by 8 grid of alternating light and dark squares.

questions.question: How many zeros are in one million?
questions.explanation: One million is written 1,000,000; a billion has nine zeros.

questions.question: Which gemstone marks a 40th wedding anniversary?
questions.explanation: Pearl marks 30 years, sapphire 45 and emerald 55.

questions.question: Which number, spelled in English, has its letters in alphabetical order?
questions.explanation: F, O, R, T, Y are in alphabetical order, the only number name like it.
questions.reviewNote: Correct for whole numbers spelled out normally; worth a quick check.

questions.question: What is a group of crows called?
questions.explanation: A parliament is a group of owls, and a murmuration is a flock of starlings.

questions.question: Which number is considered unlucky in China and Japan?
questions.explanation: In both languages, the word for four sounds like the word for death.

questions.question: What is a baby swan called?
questions.explanation: A gosling is a baby goose; cygnets are often grey and fluffy for their first year.
